title: The metabolic costs of walking and running up a 30-degree incline: implications for vertical kilometer foot races
authors: Ortiz ALR, Giovanelli N, Kram R
population: 11 experienced runners (7 M, 4 F) walking and running 5 min trials on a 30 degree treadmill incline at 0.3 m/s and rising by 0.1 m/s until failure
findings: Oxygen uptake and metabolic power increased linearly with velocity at 30 degrees.
Between 0.3 and 0.7 m/s walking cost per unit distance was lower than running cost; at 0.8 m/s there was no difference.
Extrapolation suggests that at faster velocities running likely costs less than walking.
At speeds slower than 0.7 m/s walking requires less metabolic power than running, suggesting most vertical kilometer racers should walk.
limitations: 11 runners, 5 min trials, one angle (30 degrees, about 58% grade, derived); extrapolation beyond 0.8 m/s; no fatigue.
implications: On very steep climbs (about 30 degrees) default to power hiking at the speeds most runners can sustain (below about 0.7 m/s along the slope, assuming treadmill velocity is along the belt; about 1,260 m/h of climbing, derived).
The result supports a walk-default rule for very steep grades while leaving the threshold dependent on speed.

verification.notes: Added. Crossref: Eur J Appl Physiol 117(9):1869-1876, 2017, three authors match. PubMed PMID 28695271 abstract supports all numbers; vertical-speed conversion assumes belt velocity is along the slope.
